**Surah 83: Al-Mutaffifin**

Meccan, though its status is disputed. It has thirty-six verses.

﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾. It has been said that *al-wayl* (الويل) means extreme evil. It has also been said that it means painful punishment, and that it is a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever falls for forty autumns before reaching its bottom. Other views have been reported. Whatever its meaning, it is a subject (*mubtada'*), even though it is indefinite (*nakira*), because it occurs in the position of supplication (*du'a'*). *Al-tatfif* (التطفيف, defrauding) means cheating in measuring and weighing, because what is cheated out of is a small and insignificant thing. It is reported that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina, and its people were among the most dishonest of people in measuring. So this was revealed, and they then measured well. It has also been said that when he (ﷺ) arrived there was a man there known as Abu Juhayna, who had two *sa'* measures, using one to measure out and the other to receive. It has also been said that the people of Medina were merchants who defrauded, and their transactions were *al-munabadha* (a sale by throwing a garment or stone, making the sale binding without inspection), *al-mulamasa* (a sale by touching the goods, making the touch the contract), and *al-mukhatara* (a sale involving gambling-like risk). So this was revealed, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out, recited it to them, and said: "Five for five: no people break a covenant but God sets their enemy over them; they do not rule by other than what God has sent down but poverty spreads among them; immorality does not appear among them but plague spreads among them; they do not cheat in measure but they are denied plants and seized by years of drought; and they do not withhold zakat but rain is withheld from them."

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who, when they take measure from people, take in full﴾ ...etc., is a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah kāshifah) of "the defrauders," explaining the manner of their defrauding, for which they deserved blame and the invocation of woe. That is: when they take their measure from people by way of buying and the like, they take it full and abundant. The replacement of "ʿalā" (upon) with "min" (from) is either to imply that the act of measuring (iktiyāl) contains the meaning of seizing (istīlāʾ), or to indicate that it is a measuring harmful to them. However, this is not on the basis that the harm falls within the scope of the condition contained in the word "idhā" (when), since that would disrupt the meaning, but rather in actual fact, by the requirement of the response. The intended meaning of "istīfāʾ" (taking in full) is not taking one's right in full without any shortfall, but merely taking abundantly and fully, as they wished, by whatever means were easy among the ways of tricks. They used to do this by pressing down the measure, shaking the measuring vessel, and employing trickery in filling it.

As for what has been said, that this phrasing serves to show that their measuring is for what they are owed by people, then, apart from the fact that it requires the ruling not to cover their measuring before they had anything owed to them from people by way of buying and the like, although this is the most common practice among them, it implies that the meaning of "istīfāʾ" is taking what is owed to them from them in full without shortfall. For that is what is understood from it when used absolutely in the context of a right. Thus it would not be a basis for censuring them and invoking woe upon them. And interpreting "mā lahum ʿalayhim" (what is theirs upon them) as meaning "what will be theirs upon them" (p-125), despite its being far-fetched and unprofitable, since considering that the measure is theirs, whether presently or in the future, does not necessitate that taking be in the sense mentioned as an absolute necessity. The same applies to what is reported from al-Farrāʾ, that "min" and "ʿalā" alternate in this position, because it is a right upon him; so when he says, "I measured upon you," he means "I took what is upon you," and when he says, "I measured from you," it is like his saying, "I took in full from you." So reflect.

It has also been permitted that "ʿalā" be connected to "yastawfūn" (they take in full), and that its placement before the verb serves to convey specificity (khuṣūṣiyyah), meaning: they take in full from people specifically, whereas for themselves they take in full for them (i.e., they take in full only when it is for themselves).

You know well that restriction (qaṣr) by placing the prepositional phrase before the verb occurs only where the verb can also be connected to something other than the prepositional object, according to how it is connected to it. Thus by the placement, its restriction to it is intended by way of reversal (qalb), singling out (ifrād), or specification (taʿyīn), as the context requires. There is no doubt that "istīfāʾ," which is an expression for taking one's due in full, cannot be conceived as being upon themselves, such that placing the prepositional phrase first would be intended to restrict it to people. Rather, the discourse concerns the act itself, not what the act falls upon. So reflect.

The pronoun attached in His words, exalted is He, ﴿When they measure out to them, or weigh out to them﴾, refers to the people; that is, when they measure or weigh out to others for sale or the like.

﴿they cause loss﴾, that is, they give less. It is said: "khasira al-mizan" and "akhsarahu" (he made the scale short). The preposition has been omitted and the verb made to reach its object directly, as in the verse of the poet:

"Indeed I have gathered for you akmu' (truffles) and 'asaqil (a kind of edible plant)."

That is: I have gathered for you. Making the attached pronoun a emphasis (ta'kid) for the concealed pronoun in the verb (mustakinn) is something unbecoming to the eloquence (jizalah) of the revelation. Perhaps the mention of measuring and weighing in the context of causing loss, and the restriction to "taking the measure" (iktiyal) in the context of receiving in full (istifa'), is because they were not as able to practise deception (ihtiyal) when taking as they were when measuring and weighing. Also, the absence of mention of what is measured or weighed in both cases is because the context of the speech is to explain the badness of their dealings in taking and giving, not the specific nature of what is taken or given.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 4:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that comes to magnify the enormity of what they committed of defrauding (tatfif), and to express amazement at their audacity in it. "Ulaika" (those) is a demonstrative referring to the defrauders (al-Mutaffifin). Placing it in the position of their pronoun serves to signal the basis of the ruling, which is their attribute, for indicating a thing by a demonstrative points to it with regard to its being characterized by its attribute, whereas the pronoun does not point to its attribute. It also serves to announce that they are distinguished by that ugly attribute from the rest of people in the most complete distinction, placing them in the station of things pointed to by a sensory demonstration. The sense of distance contained in it (the demonstrative) signals the distance of their rank in wickedness and corruption. That is: Do not those described by that dreadful, appalling, and abominable attribute think that they will be resurrected?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 5:

﴿For a momentous Day﴾. Its magnitude cannot be measured, nor the magnitude of what it contains, and they will be called to account on it for the weight of an atom and a mustard seed. For whoever supposes this, even if it is a weak supposition bordering on doubt and illusion, scarcely dares to commit such vile deeds. So how about one who is certain of it?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 6:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ (p-126)

That is: for His judgment and His decree. It is in the accusative by an implied "I mean" (a'ni). It has also been said that it is governed by "mab'uthun" (resurrected), or that it is in the nominative position as a predicate of an implied subject, or that it is in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for "a Great Day," built on the fath (fatha) vowel because it is attached to a verb, even though the verb is in the present tense, as is the view of the Kufans. The last two readings are supported by the recitation in the nominative and in the genitive. In this there is denial, astonishment, the mention of supposition, the description of the day as great, the standing of people in it all together before God, humbled, and the description of Him, exalted is He, with lordship over the worlds, is a clear statement of the greatness of the sin and the enormity of the offense in cheating in measure and the like, which is not hidden.

﴿No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is surely in Sijjin.﴾

"No!" is a rebuke (radʿ) against what they were doing, namely defrauding in measure (al-tatfif) and heedlessness of the Resurrection (al-baʿth) and the Reckoning (al-ḥisab). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾, etc., is a justification for the rebuke, or for the necessity of restraint, established by way of verification.

"Sijjin" (سِجِّينٌ) is a proper name for a comprehensive register, the ledger of evil, in which are recorded the deeds of the devils and the deeds of the disbelievers and the sinners from the two weighty groups (al-thaqalan), jinn and humankind. It is transferred from an adjective, like khatam (خاتَم), and its original form is fiʿʿīl (فِعِّيل), derived from al-sijn, which means confinement and constriction, either because it is the cause of confinement and constriction in Hell, or because it is cast, as it is said, beneath the seventh earth in a dark, desolate place, which is the dwelling of Iblis and his offspring.

So the meaning is: indeed the record of the wicked, among whom are the defrauders, that is, what is written of their deeds, or the writing of their deeds, is in that register, which records the vile deeds of those mentioned.
Divine saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ It is an emphasis on its magnitude, meaning: it is of such a nature that the knowledge of no one reaches it.

Abu al-Su'ud's Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 83, verse 9:

As for His saying, ﴿a written record﴾, meaning: inscribed, its writing clearly set down; or marked, such that whoever sees it knows that there is no good in it. It has been said that it is a noun of place, and the implied meaning is: "What is the register of the prisoners?" or "a place of a written record."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Woe on that day to those who deny﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾. What lies between them is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) with His saying, exalted is He: *

Translation:

﴿Those who deny the Day of Judgment﴾ may be in the genitive case as a disparaging attribute (ṣifah dhāmmah) of "the deniers," or as a substitute (badal) for it, or in the nominative or accusative case by way of disparagement (dhamm).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 12:

﴿And none deny it except every transgressor﴾ i.e., one who exceeds the limits of reflection and consideration, who is excessive in taqlid (blind imitation of authority), to the point that he deems the power and knowledge of God Most High insufficient for the resurrection, even while he witnesses the original creation.

﴿Sinful﴾ i.e., one who is immersed in the base and perishable desires, such that they preoccupy him from what lies beyond them of complete and lasting pleasures, and drive him to deny them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 13:

﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, the verses that state this (i.e., the verses explicitly declaring it).

﴿He says﴾ out of the extremity of his ignorance and his turning away from the truth, from which there is no escape.

﴿Tales of the ancients﴾: that is, they are the stories of the ancients. Al-Kalbi said: the one meant by "the transgressor, the sinner" is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was also said: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. And it was said: it is general, applying to everyone who is characterized by the attributes mentioned. It was also read as "idha yutla" with the verb in the masculine form, and it was read as "a-idha tutla" in the form of a rhetorical, disapproving interrogation.

Kallā (no! / far from it) is a rebuke to the transgressor, the sinner, for that false statement, and a denial of it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, rather, what they have been earning has rusted over their hearts.﴾ is an explanation of what led them to utter that monstrous saying. That is, there is nothing in Our verses that could rightly be said about them like these false sayings. Rather, (ra-ka-ba, "mounted") over their hearts and overcame them what they had been earning of disbelief and sins, until they became like rust on a mirror. That prevented them from knowing the truth. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whenever the servant commits a sin, a black spot is placed on his heart, until his heart becomes black." Therefore they said what they said.

Al-Rayn (rust) is al-sada' (rust, corrosion). It is said: "The sin rained (ran) upon him, and it covered him with rayn and ghayn." It is also said: "Sleep ran upon him," meaning it became firmly settled in him. It is also recited with the assimilation of the lam into the ra' (i.e., "bal rrana").

"Nay" (kalla) is a rebuke and a deterrence from the sinful earning (al-kasb al-rayn).

"Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day" (﴿إنَّهم عَنْ رَبِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ لَمَحْجُوبُونَ﴾). Therefore they will scarcely be able to see Him, unlike the believers. It has also been said that this is an image (tamthil) for their humiliation, by way of the humiliation of one who is kept from entering upon kings. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Mulaykah that it means: veiled from His mercy; and from Ibn Kaysan, that it means: veiled from His honour.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 16:

﴿Then indeed they will be burning in the Blazing Fire.﴾ That is: they will enter the Fire. "Then" (thumma) indicates the distance in rank; for the burning of the Blazing Fire is more severe than the humiliation and deprivation of mercy and honor.

Then it is said [to them], as rebuke and reproach, from the direction of the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniyah):

﴿This is what you used to deny﴾, so taste its punishment.

Kallā (﴿كَلا﴾): a rebuke against what they were upon, a rebuke following another rebuke, a deterrent following a deterrent. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾ is a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) brought to clarify the station of the record of the righteous. After it comes the clarification of the evil condition of the wicked, linked to the clarification of the evil condition of their record. In it is an emphasis on the rebuke and on the obligation to be restrained (al-irtidāʿ).

"Their record" (kitābuhum): what was written of their deeds. "ʿIlliyyūn" (ʿIlliyyūn): a proper name for the register of good (dīwān al-khayr) in which is recorded everything the angels and the righteous among jinn and humankind (al-thaqalayn) have done. It is a proper noun transferred from the plural of the form faʿīl, derived from al-ʿuluww (height). It was so named either because it is the cause of ascending to the highest ranks in Paradise, or because it is raised up in the seventh heaven, where the Karrūbiyyūn (the cherubim) dwell, as an honour to it and a magnification of it.
(p-128) The discussion concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ is as has passed concerning its counterpart.
(p-128) The discussion concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ is as has passed concerning its counterpart.

The words of Allah Most High, ﴿Witnessed by those brought near (to Allah)﴾, are another attribute of "Book" (kitab). That is: they attend it and guard it, or they bear witness to what is in it on the Day of Resurrection.

Verse 22: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾. This begins an explanation of the excellent conditions of the righteous, following the account of their record, in the same manner as what came earlier concerning the wicked.

On the couches [ʿalā al-arāʾik], i.e., on the beds within the canopies (al-ḥijāl). Among them the term arīka is hardly applied to a bed except when it is within a canopy (ḥajala).

They gaze [yanẓurūn], i.e., except what they wish of extending their eyes toward it of the desirable sights of Paradise, and toward what Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon them of blessing and honor, and toward their enemies being punished in the Fire; and the canopies do not block their sight from perceiving.

You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss (ﷺ no)—

Let me correct that: the passage contains no ﷺ, so no honorific applies here. The translation follows.

You will recognize in their faces the radiance of delight: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾. That is, the brightness of enjoying pleasure, its sheen and its luster. The address is to everyone who has a share in being addressed, to signal that the marks of blessing and the signs of joy that they possess are such that seeing them is not restricted to one viewer over another.
﴿They will be given to drink of [a] ﴾ **raḥīq** (pure, choice wine) — a pure drink, with no adulteration in it — ﴿sealed﴾.

**Verse 83:26** — ﴿Its seal is musk.﴾ That is, its vessels and cups are sealed with musk in place of clay. Perhaps this is a figurative expression for the completeness of its excellence. It was also said: "Its seal is musk" means its final part (its end) is a scent of musk. It is read as "khātamuhu" with a fatḥa and with a kasra on the tā', meaning that by which it is sealed and closed off.

﴿And for that﴾ is a reference to the wine (al-raḥīq), and this is the more fitting reading in light of what follows. Or it refers to what has been mentioned of their states. The sense of distance in the demonstrative may either indicate the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its station, or be due to its being in Paradise; that is, for that alone and nothing else.

﴿So let those who compete compete﴾ means: let those who desire eagerly hasten to obedience to God, the Exalted. It was also said: let those who act act, as in His saying, ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾. It was also said: let those who race race. The root of tanāfus (competition) is rivalry over a precious thing, and its root is from nafs (self, soul) because of its preciousness. Al-Wāḥidī said: "I valued the thing, I hold it precious (anfusuhu nafāsatan), and tanāfus is its reciprocal form, as if each of the two persons wants to have it exclusively for himself." Al-Baghawī said: its root is from the precious thing that people's souls covet, each one desires it for his own self, and is stingy with it toward others, that is, he begrudges it.

And its mixture is from Tasnim.

And its mixture is from Tasnim. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "its seal" (khitāmuhu) and is another attribute of "rahīq" (sealed wine), like it; and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ) that affirms its excellence. That is: what is mixed with the rahīq is water from Tasnim, and "min" here is either explanatory (bayaniyyah) or partitive (tabʿiḍiyyah), or it is "min nafsihi" (from itself), taking "min" as the ibtidaʾiyyah (of origin). "Tasnim" is a proper name (ʿalam) for a particular spring (ʿayn), named thus either because it is the highest drink in Paradise, or because it comes to them from above. It is reported that it flows through the air, elevated (mutasannimah), and then pours into their vessels.

"ʿAynan" (عَيْنًا) is in the accusative of specialization (*al-ikhtisās*, a construction in which a noun is singled out for emphasis). It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) describing "tasnīm" (تَسْنِيمٍ), even though the latter is a fixed noun (*jāmid*), because it is described by it. His, the Exalted's, statement:

"Drinking from it will be those brought near (to God)."

For they drink it pure, while it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise. So the "bi" (بِ) is either superfluous (*zāʾidah*) or means "min" (from).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ ...etc., is a narration of some of the ugly deeds of the polytheists of Quraysh, brought in as a preface to the mention of some of the conditions of the righteous in Paradise.

﴿used to be﴾ in the worldly life.

﴿of those who believed, laughing﴾ meaning: they would mock their poor, such as ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Khabbab, Bilal and others among the poor believers. The placing of the prepositional phrase first (min alladhina amanu, "of those who believed") is either for restriction (qasr), to indicate the extreme ugliness of what they did, meaning: they used to laugh at those who believed, even though it was clear that they did not deserve that, following the pattern of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾; or it is for the sake of observing the fawasil (the verse-endings).

"And when they passed by them": that is, the poor among the believers.

"By them": that is, by the disbelievers, while they were in their gatherings. This is the more apparent reading, though the reverse is also permissible.

"They winked at one another": that is, some of them nudged others, and they gestured with their eyes.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 31:**

﴿And when they returned﴾ from their gatherings.

﴿to their own people, they returned jesting﴾, delighting in speaking ill of them and mocking them. In this there is an indication that they would not do this in the sight of those who passed by them, and would then suffice themselves with winking (al-taghamuz).

It is also read as "fākihīn" (fākihīn). It has been said: both mean the same thing. It has been said: "fakihīn" means exultant (ashirīn), and it has been said: joyful (fariḥīn), and "fākihīn" means "mutafakkihīn" (those who delight in jest). It has been said: pampered (nā'imīn), and it has been said: joking (māzihīn).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 32:

﴿And when they see them﴾ wherever they are.

﴿They say, "Indeed, these are surely astray."﴾ That is: they attributed error to the Muslims, both those they saw and others, by means of emphasis (ta'kid).

**Qur'anic quotation:** ﴿وَما أُرْسِلُوا عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ — "Yet they had not been sent as guardians over them."

"Over them" refers to the believers (al-Muslimun).

﴿حافِظِينَ﴾ — "as guardians" — is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the waw of "qalu" (they said). That is, they said this while the reality was that they had not been sent from God Most High as those entrusted with them, guarding over their conditions, watching over their deeds, and bearing witness to their rightness and their error. This is a mockery of them and an indication that what they boldly said is among the duties of one who is sent from Him, Exalted is He.

It has also been permitted that this be part of the speech of the criminals (al-mujrimun), as if they said: "Indeed these people are astray, and they have not been sent as guardians over us," denying that these believers should turn them away from polytheism and call them to Islam. The phrase "ʿalayhim" (over them) is used here as a report of the meaning (naql lahu bi'l-ma'na), not of the wording, just as in your saying: "He swore that he would certainly do it" (ḥalafa li-yafʿalanna), not with the exact wording as in your saying: "He swore: 'I will certainly do it'" (ḥalafa li-afʿalanna).

Verse 34: ﴿So today those who believed⁠﴾, that is, the aforementioned poor (al-ma'hudun min al-fuqara').

﴿from the disbelievers⁠﴾, that is, from the aforementioned (al-ma'hudin) — and this is the more apparent reading — though it is possible to take it generally from both sides (al-tan'im min al-janibayn).

﴿laugh⁠﴾ when they see them humiliated and shackled, overcome by all kinds of disgrace and abasement after might and arrogance, and overtaken by various torments after luxury and comfort. The placing of the prepositional phrase first (taqdim al-jar wa'l-majrur) is for restriction (al-qasr), realizing the antithesis (li'l-muqabala): that is, today it is they (the believers) who laugh at the disbelievers, not the disbelievers at them, as they used to do in the world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 83, verse 35:

And His saying, ﴿Upon couches, looking﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of "yadhakun" (they laugh): that is, they laugh at them, looking at them and at the wretched state they are in. It was also said: a door to the Garden is opened for the disbelievers, and they are told, "Come out to it." But when they reach it, it is shut in their faces. This is done to them repeatedly, and the believers laugh at them.

And his saying, exalted is He, refutes this: ﴿Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?﴾ For it is explicit that the believers' laughing at them is a recompense for their laughing at the believers in this world. Therefore there must necessarily be correspondence (*mujanasa*) and conformity (*mushakala*) between them. *Tathwib* and *ithaba* mean recompense. It was also read with the assimilation (*idgham*, merging one letter into the next) of the *lam* into the *tha'*.

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Mutaffifin, Allah will give him to drink on the Day of Resurrection from the sealed nectar (*al-raheeq al-makhtum*)."
